parts: A town. A piper. Rats. Unpaid debt. Then: one hundred thirty children, gone forever.
That's the story everyone knows about Hamelin, Germany, in the year twelve eighty-four.
But the oldest sources that survive don't mention rats at all.
Not one.
So where did the rats come from?
And what's actually documented about this legend?
We'll mark it all: documented, disputed, or myth.
By the end, you'll see this isn't one story — it's layers, added over three hundred years.
The real mystery isn't just what happened to the children. It's how the story itself changed.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
Here's the version everyone repeats.
Hamelin has a rat problem. A piper offers to clear it, for payment. He plays, the rats follow him into the river Weser, and drown.
The town refuses to pay. The piper returns, plays a different tune, and leads one hundred thirty children away. They're never seen again.
Now, the documented part.
The oldest known depiction of this legend is a stained-glass window in Hamelin's market church, made around the year thirteen hundred.
It was destroyed in sixteen sixty. What we know of it comes from written descriptions, by visitors, centuries later.
And that window shows a piper leading children away. No rats.
The oldest surviving written account is a note from around fourteen forty, kept in the town archive of Luneburg.
It also describes a piper, taking children.
Still no rats.
So when do the rats show up?
Not until a chronicle written between fifteen fifty-nine and fifteen sixty-five — at least one hundred twenty years after the earliest sources.
That means "rats, unpaid piper, missing children," as one single story, is a layer added by later generations.
It's not what the earliest records describe.
So where do the numbers come from? One hundred thirty children. June twenty-sixth, twelve eighty-four.
From an inscription on a building in Hamelin's market square: the Rat Catcher's House.
Here's the catch. That house was built in sixteen oh two, sixteen oh three — more than three hundred years after the date it records.
It's a real inscription. It's just not a document from the time of the events.
And the dates don't even agree with each other.

Robert Browning's famous eighteen forty-two poem uses the year thirteen seventy-six, not twelve eighty-four. One writer even cited fourteen eighty-four, with no source at all — and historians have called that one out directly.
So even the "official" date is disputed.
Historians have proposed real explanations for what lies underneath the legend.
A natural disaster. A plague, with the piper as a symbol of death.
A recruitment or crusade of young people, sometimes loosely linked to a real medieval battle fought near Hamelin in twelve fifty-nine.
A case of dance mania — the compulsive dancing outbreaks recorded elsewhere in that era.

And the most cited modern theory: a linguist traced family names and place names from medieval Hamelin to regions resettled far to the east. In this reading, the piper wasn't a sorcerer — he was a recruiter for emigration.
It's the best-supported theory so far. It is not proven. None of these six explanations is confirmed.
Even Hamelin's own town government says so.
Its official website states plainly that the truth behind the legend has eluded historians to this day, and that no one can prove what happened.
The town museum agrees: the historical core still can't be fully clarified.
One popular version even sends the children to Transylvania.
Hamelin's own tourism page calls that one folklore — it doesn't match the emigration evidence at all.
So here's what's documented: a piper, leading children away, recorded within about a century of the date given.
Here's what's disputed: the exact number, the exact year, and every explanation offered since.
And here's the myth: that the rats were ever part of the original story.
So if this story kept changing — what else have we been told was "the original version," when it never was?
